notes:
I've organised these notes verse by verse, with the URL after each point. A few things to know first:

- **Sources:** I fully read Enduring Word (Guzik), Ellicott (on Bible Hub) and part of Precept Austin's chapter page. Everything else comes from the Bible Hub and StudyLight commentary pages, which collect Gill, Pulpit, Barnes, Calvin, Henry, JFB, Keil & Delitzsch and others. Enduring Word and Ellicott are cited by URL only, with no sentence references.
- **Tradition labels:** The labels (Calvin as Reformed, Gill as Baptist, Ellicott as Anglican, Henry as Presbyterian/Nonconformist) are mine. The pages themselves don't use them.
- **Gaps:** I found nothing on these verses from Methodist/Wesleyan, Lutheran, Orthodox or Pentecostal sites, from NET Bible notes or Bible Odyssey, or from prosperity or word-of-faith teaching. Those are left out, as you asked.

---

**v. 1**
- Precept Austin points out that the book isn't in time order: this chapter's events actually come after those in Jeremiah 37. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary
- Guzik: Zedekiah was the last king before Babylon's final conquest, which began in his tenth year. He quotes Harrison: the siege began in Zedekiah's ninth year, was briefly lifted when Egypt's army approached, then resumed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/
- Ellicott dates this to 589 BC. He says Zedekiah's scheming foreign policy had provoked the siege. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/32.htm
- Matthew Henry: God's judgments came gradually upon them, but, they not meeting him by repentance in the way of his judgments, he proceeded in his controversy till all was laid waste. That happened in the eleventh year. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-5.html

**v. 2**
- Guzik quotes Feinberg: the "courtyard of the guard" was probably a stockade in the palace grounds for prisoners, and friends could visit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/
- Ellicott agrees that visitors were allowed. Drawing on Jer 37–38, he says Jeremiah had earlier been held in the house of Jonathan the scribe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/32.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch fill in the sequence. Jeremiah was seized and thrown into a dungeon, on the pretence that he intended to go over to the Chaldeans. Later Zedekiah moved him to the court of the prison-house, where he remained in confinement till the city was taken. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-5.htm

**v. 3**
- Guzik quotes Feinberg: Zedekiah locked Jeremiah up even while watching his predictions come true, which is "the irrationality of unbelief." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/
- Henry: Silencing God's prophets, though it is not so bad as mocking and killing them, is yet a great affront to the God of heaven. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-5.html
- Ellicott: comparing Jer 34 and 38 shows Jeremiah never changed his message. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/32.htm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: Nebuchadnezzar later blinded Zedekiah, which gives the words "eye to eye" special force. The face of the great king, in all the terror of his wrath, was to be the last object Zedekiah was to behold on earth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/32.htm
- Bible.org (Utley): the phrase is a Hebrew idiom for a personal encounter. 2 Kings 25 records that Zedekiah's family was killed in front of him before he was blinded. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21206
- Guzik quotes Trapp: Zedekiah had to face the king he had betrayed despite his oath. Trapp then applies this to sinners standing before the King of kings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/

**v. 5 — "until I attend to (visit) him": the main point of disagreement**
- Ellicott (Anglican): the word can mean punishing or delivering. Its use in 29:10 points to deliverance here, and Jeremiah seems to cherish the hope that he will not be altogether excluded. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-5.htm
- Barnes: it means In the sense of punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-5.html
- JFB reads it in a good sense: it refers to the honour paid Zedekiah at his death and burial (Jeremiah 34:4-5). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/jeremiah-32.html
- Gill (Baptist): it means God taking Zedekiah away by a natural death, which given his blinding and captivity might be reckoned a visitation in mercy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-5.htm
- Geneva Bible notes (Reformed): Till I take Zedekiah away by death: for he will not die by the sword. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-5.htm
- Calvin (Reformed) sees some alleviation was promised, if indeed a certain kind of death may be deemed a favor. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-5.html
- Pulpit: the word is used both ways, so that no definite announcement is made respecting Zedekiah's future. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-5.htm
- Poole says interpreters are divided between judgment and mercy. He rejects the idea that Zedekiah lived on until the return from exile, because he would have been about 92. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-5.htm
- Coffman and Constable read it negatively. Coffman says it does not seem to indicate any such thing as blessing. Constable takes it as evidently with death. Precept Austin also reads it negatively. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-5.html
- Early church: Jerome, cited in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary, called the words puzzling, since "visitation means both *consolation* and *punishment*." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-32.html
- Text note: Cambridge says the phrase and the rest of the verse are lacking in the LXX, the Greek Old Testament. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-5.htm

**vv. 6–7**
- Guzik: Hanamel offers the field by "right of redemption." The land had to stay in the family, so it had to be offered to Jeremiah first, as in Ruth 4:6. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Jer/Jer-32.cfm
- Guzik: Anathoth was about three miles from Jerusalem, and Jeremiah was offered the purchase of land that was *already* under Babylonian control. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/
- Ellicott tackles the legal question, since priestly land couldn't be sold (Lev 25:34). He suggests the land came into the family by marriage, or that only use until the next Jubilee was transferred. He compares this "redeemer" role to Ruth 3–4. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/32.htm
- JFB: the ban only stopped land passing from Levites to another tribe. What was bought here is only the purchase of the use of the field till the year of jubilee. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/jfb/jer/jer_032.cfm

**v. 8**
- Guzik: Hanamel's visit happened just as God said, and from that Jeremiah knew it **was the word of the LORD**. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/
- On guidance, Guzik quotes G. Campbell Morgan: God's word seems to have come as an impression, as it so often comes to us, and When the call is followed by the open door, we need have no hesitation. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/archives/guzik_david/StudyGuide2017-Jer/Jer-32.cfm
- Ellicott compares the confirming visit to the arrival of Cornelius's messengers for Peter (Acts 10). He also guesses at Hanamel's motives: the field may have been ruined by the army, or he may have wanted it owned by someone the Babylonians would protect. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/32.htm
- Guzik quotes Kidner ("Was there ever a more insensitive prison-visitor?") and Ryken on Leviticus 25 land law. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: the Hebrew literally reads "seven shekels and ten [pieces of] silver." The price seems far below market value. He tentatively suggests 7 × 10 may echo the 70 years of exile. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/32.htm
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: the purchase was "utterly valueless" by any prudent standard. In Spurgeon's view Jeremiah was "preaching by what he did." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/
- Henry: Jeremiah was very honest and exact in paying the money. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-14.html

**vv. 10–11**
- Ellicott: the detail shows Jeremiah left out no legal step. Money was weighed rather than counted, probably to guard against clipped coins. He gives two theories for the sealed and open copies: simple duplicates, or a second document with terms the witnesses didn't need to see. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/32.htm
- Guzik quotes Thompson: in Jewish Elephantine (Egypt) practice, a contract was folded, tied and sealed, with an open copy attached. Similar deeds have been found in the Judean desert. He also quotes Harrison: the legal steps were followed "as though the land were at peace." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/
- JFB: "law and custom" may refer to the law of redemption, so that after the return the deed would show Jeremiah bought as next of kin. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/jfb/jer/jer_032.cfm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: this is Baruch's first appearance. Naming his father and grandfather suggests a noble family; his brother Seraiah held high rank, and Josephus calls the family illustrious. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/32.htm
- Guzik: the deal was conducted in public before witnesses, all according to custom, even from prison. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/

**vv. 13–15**
- Guzik: the clay jar worked as a time capsule. He quotes Cundall on the parallel with the Dead Sea Scrolls. He quotes Kidner: the care taken over the deeds was an affirmation "as solid as the silver that paid for it" that God would restore. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/
- Wiersbe: Jeremiah had to practise God's promises as well as preach them, so this was an "action sermon" at Judah's lowest point. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary
- Henry: just as staying unmarried confirmed Jeremiah's warnings of ruin, buying the field confirm[ed] his predictions of the future restoration of Jerusalem. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-14.html
- Ellicott compares a Roman who bought land at full price while Hannibal's army marched on Rome (Livy). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/32.htm

**v. 16**
- JFB: Jeremiah couldn't see how God's threat fit with this command, so he turned to his grand remedy against perplexities, prayer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/jfb/jer/jer_032.cfm
- Bible.org: apparently he still had some degree of doubt. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21206
- Guzik quotes Trapp: a man "may pray away his perturbations." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/
- Ryken (quoted by Precept Austin): Jeremiah gave far more of the prayer to praise than to his problem. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary

**v. 17**
- Ellicott: The thought of the omnipotence of God was here, as always, the ground of prayer. The same phrase appears in Genesis 18:14. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/32-17.htm
- Pulpit: "Ah" is better rendered "Alas!", as in 1:6. "Too hard" is the word usually translated "wonderful," meaning something outside the ordinary. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-17.htm
- Calvin: praising God's power kept Jeremiah humble, so that he would not dare to clamor against God. The Hebrew can mean "wonderful" or "hidden." Most older interpreters took it as "nothing is hidden from you," but Calvin also accepts Jerome's "nothing is difficult." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-17.html
- Text note: Gill says the Targum (the Aramaic paraphrase) reads "hidden from thee." The Greek Old Testament reads nothing can be hidden from thee. https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/32-17.htm
- Cambridge: "outstretched arm" here refers to creation (as in 27:5); elsewhere it refers to God's acts of deliverance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-17.htm
- F. B. Meyer: a God who made heaven and earth could easily drive out the Chaldeans and restore normal land ownership. Precept Austin also quotes Spurgeon's sermon on the verse. Its editor adds a comment about believing in a literal seven-day creation; that is the website's own view, not part of the commentators' explanation of the verse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary

**v. 18 — "iniquity of the fathers into the laps of their children": a real difference between traditions**
- Calvin (Reformed): the innocent aren't punished, because this applies to the wicked. Part of the punishment is that God withholds from them his Spirit. He rejects the view that only temporal (earthly) punishment is meant. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-18.html
- Gill (Baptist): he connects this with the Ten Commandments' "of them that hate me" and the Targum's addition. Children are punished when they imitate their fathers in their wickedness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-18.htm
- Geneva notes (Reformed): descendants under the curse "by nature" are punished both for their own sin and for their fathers' iniquity, "which is likewise in them." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-18.htm
- Ellicott (Anglican): the words echo Exodus 34:7. He sees retribution working through the continuity of family and national life, which the "sour grapes" proverb (31:29) caricatured. He also sees a mercy which is wider than that retribution, and at last triumphant. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-18.htm
- Henry: His reprieves are not pardons. God may spare parents in order to lead them to repentance, yet still repay their sin on their children and yet does them no wrong. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-18.html
- A modern evangelical note on Bible Hub frames this as Consequences, not fatalism, adding that individual accountability still stands (31:30). https://biblehub.com/jeremiah/32-18.htm
- Background: Barnes and Pulpit explain "bosom" as the folds of an Eastern garment, which worked as a pocket. Ellicott links "Mighty God" with Isaiah 9:6. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/32-18.htm

**v. 19**
- Henry: God contrives every thing for the best, and effects every thing as he contrived it, and so such a God as this is not to be quarrelled with. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-17.html
- Ryken: Jeremiah had just been reminded that God knows everything, since God knew all about the visit even before it happened. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary
- Guzik: verses 18–19 move from God's mercy to God's justice and judgment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-32/

**vv. 20–21**
- Ryken: having praised God as Creator, Jeremiah now recounts God as Redeemer. Kidner adds that Christians can include the greatest redemptive act of all. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary
- Henry: God brought Israel out of Egypt with glory to himself, with signs and wonders, witness the ten plagues, and with a strong hand, too strong for the Egyptians themselves. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-17.html
- Bridgeway: Jeremiah reminds God of his steadfast faithfulness and miraculous power, which had saved his people in the past (20-22). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/32-17.html

**v. 22**
- Rosscup: "this land" is the land God swore to Israel, which the field purchase illustrates. in integrity it can be no other than that very land. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary
- Where Protestants differ (these comments are on the chapter's later promises, which bear on "this land"): Precept Austin argues for a literal future fulfilment for Israel, unless one holds the false belief that God is finished with Israel. Ryken, quoted on the same page, applies the promises to the church, the bride of Christ, the true Israel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_32_commentary
- Catholic reading: the Knox translation on New Advent heads the chapter as foretelling the people's return and the everlasting covenant God will make with his Church. https://www.newadvent.org/bible/jer032.htm
